406: The total colour difference is a composite of the three colour coordinates, so that its behaviour follows arithmetically from theirs and it contributes no independent information. The large increase between fresh and stored grain is driven almost entirely by the rise in yellowness and the movement away from green that accompany post-harvest curing. The more informative observation is the plateau that followed: once the initial transition was complete, overall colour held steady for the remainder of the year, which accords with the stability of the individual coordinates reported by Yanxia et al. (2018). For the trade the implication is that stored aromatic rice is unlikely to be rejected on colour within a year, provided moisture is controlled. The differences between growing sites most probably reflect the distance at which each lot began from the reference colour rather than any difference in the rate of curing. A single composite index of this kind affords a convenient basis for objective grading (Kumaresh et al., 2020).

432: Copper concentration was unaffected by storage, precisely as theory predicts, since mineral elements are neither synthesised nor lost from intact grain held under ambient conditions. This outcome serves as a useful internal check, indicating that the analytical procedure was sound and that the changes recorded for other traits represent real effects rather than laboratory drift. Grain mineral concentration is established during the growing season by root uptake and translocation to the developing panicle, so that the differences between sites are most probably attributable to the copper status of the three soils and to the chemical conditions governing its availability to the plant. That the landrace ranking altered from one site to another suggests that the three differ in the efficiency with which they absorb copper from different soils, and no single landrace can therefore be recommended as the superior accumulator without specification of the soil. Li et al. (2018) similarly found grain composition to respond jointly to genotype and to the conditions of the growing area.

452: Iron deficiency ranks among the most widespread nutritional problems in India, and rice is a poor source of the element, so the wide varietal differences recorded here carry practical interest and identify the leading landrace as a candidate for work directed at raising grain iron (Perera et al., 2018). As anticipated for a mineral, storage exerted no effect. That stability should be read alongside the decline in phytic acid over the same period, since phytate constitutes the principal barrier to the absorption of non-haem iron; as the ratio of phytate to iron improves, aged grain should deliver more available iron notwithstanding that its total iron is unchanged (Fukushima et al., 2020). The differences between growing sites most probably reflect the contrasting soils of the state, iron being more available in lateritic than in alluvial soils. The reversal of the landrace ranking between sites constitutes a caution against inferring grain iron from a single location, and is consistent with the strong influence of growing area on grain composition reported by Li et al. (2018).

472: Zinc, like iron, is frequently deficient in diets founded upon rice, and the grain again proved a modest source. Storage exerted no effect, as anticipated for a mineral, and the marginal statistical separation between sampling dates reflects the low experimental error rather than any genuine change in the grain. The varietal ranking ran counter to that for iron, which most probably indicates that the two elements are absorbed and deposited by at least partly independent routes within the plant; no single landrace among the three combines superiority for both, so that a breeder seeking to raise them together would be obliged to recombine them. The differences between growing sites are most probably an effect of soil chemistry, since zinc becomes less available to rice in soils that are alkaline, high in phosphorus or maintained under prolonged flooding, and the site returning the most phytic acid, itself the phosphorus reserve of the seed, returned the least zinc. As with iron, the decline in phytate during storage should improve the proportion of zinc absorbable by the body (Perera et al., 2018; Fukushima et al., 2020).
